title: Handling Production Issues
description: Tests whether engineers respond to production failures with accountable diagnosis, clear communication, safe mitigation, and durable learning.

competency.name: Production Ownership
competency.definition: Protects customers during production problems through calm investigation, clear communication, accountable mitigation, and prevention.
competency.whyItMatters: Production failures reveal whether engineers understand impact, communicate honestly, reduce risk safely, and learn from the failure instead of only fixing the immediate symptom.

prompt.primary: Tell me about a time you caused or helped resolve a production incident.
variants: Describe a time when you had to debug a difficult production problem.
Tell me about a time you improved observability, reliability, or performance.
Describe a time something failed after release and the impact was not obvious at first.
Tell me about a time your own change caused a production issue.
Describe a time when the first mitigation fixed one symptom but left another risk.
Describe a time when you pushed back on a risky production mitigation.
interviewerIntent: Can the candidate stay calm and structured when impact is real?
Do they communicate uncertainty and customer impact clearly?
Do they turn the incident into better tests, observability, rollout, or operational habits?
Can they own their part in causing or prolonging the incident without turning the story into blame or self-protection?
Can they explain rejected mitigations, residual customer impact, and the risk that still needed closure?
Can they push back on an unsafe fast fix while still offering a concrete path to recovery?

scenario.signatureExample: An engineer helps resolve a checkout latency spike triggered by their release, communicates impact before root cause is certain, then improves rollback criteria, dashboards, and ownership for the dependency.
context: The incident begins as intermittent latency and does not immediately point to a single service.
Product and support need usable updates before root cause is fully understood.
A rollback may reduce customer pain but also remove diagnostic evidence or create downstream cleanup.
The candidate may have authored, reviewed, or approved the change that triggered the issue.
Customer impact may remain after service dashboards recover, such as stale data, delayed jobs, or confusing status-page history.
A stakeholder may pressure the team toward a fast manual production change before the blast radius and rollback path are understood.
constraints: The team must balance mitigation speed with diagnostic confidence.
Updates must be honest about uncertainty while still useful to non-engineers.
Follow-up work must reduce future detection or recovery time, not just document the incident.
The candidate must separate accountable ownership from personal blame or defensive explanation.
Mitigation choices may trade recovery speed against data integrity, diagnostic evidence, or support workload.
Pushback on a risky mitigation should be specific and evidence-based, not a vague attempt to avoid responsibility.

storyAnatomy.situation: A production problem affected customers, internal operators, or a critical workflow after the candidate's change, a team release, or a latent system weakness.
storyAnatomy.task: Help restore or contain the service, communicate status, understand root cause, and prevent recurrence at the right scope.
action: First established impact, affected segment, severity, and current owner before deep debugging.
Named the candidate's own contribution to the trigger or response delay without making the incident about personal guilt.
Used logs, metrics, traces, recent deploys, and customer examples to narrow the search rather than guessing.
Communicated what was known, unknown, and next update time to support, product, or incident channels.
Chose or recommended rollback, flag disablement, throttling, data correction, or fix-forward with explicit trade-offs.
Rejected at least one tempting action, such as a blind rollback, direct database edit, noisy global alert, or broad rewrite, and explained the larger risk.
Escalated or paused an unsafe production action by naming a safer path, decision owner, validation plan, and customer-impact update.
Helped run a blameless review that separated trigger, contributing factors, detection gaps, and prevention work.
result: Customer impact stopped or degraded behavior was contained, with the affected group identified within a defined window.
The team could explain root cause and contributing factors without hiding uncertainty.
Residual data loss, delayed jobs, manual cleanup, or customer communication debt was made visible with an owner.
Detection, rollback, runbook, test coverage, or ownership improved after the incident.
storyAnatomy.reflection: The main learning was that production ownership means protecting customers while preserving enough evidence to learn, not only debugging quickly.
systemChange: Dashboard and alert tied to customer-visible symptoms, not only service health or error rate.
Release checklist with rollback criteria and feature-flag owner.
Rollback and fix-forward decision guide that names when to preserve evidence, when to stop customer pain immediately, and who decides.
Incident review template that tracks action items to verified completion.
Runbook for the affected dependency or failure mode.
Production data-change checklist with dry-run output, peer review, rollback or reconciliation plan, and named approval threshold.
Post-incident action tracker that verifies whether detection, customer correction, and support communication actually closed.

exampleStories.title: Checkout Latency Spike
exampleStories.promptVariant: Tell me about a time you caused or helped resolve a production incident.
exampleStories.situation: The engineer shipped a release that changed how checkout called a promotions service. Thirty minutes later, p95 checkout latency doubled for customers using stacked discounts, but service dashboards still looked green because error rates were low.
strongAnswerSketch: Join the incident channel with the deploy timeline, affected endpoint, customer-visible latency chart, and a clear note that their own change was the likely trigger.
Compare traces before and after release, identify the new sequential promotions calls, and recommend disabling the flag while preserving trace samples.
Post clear updates that distinguish confirmed latency from unconfirmed revenue impact, and ask support to tag discount-related checkout tickets separately.
After recovery, add a checkout-latency alert, a performance test for promotion-heavy carts, and a release checklist item for external calls.
whyItWorks: Shows accountability for the candidate's own release even though the symptom was latency rather than a clean error.
Uses evidence to support mitigation instead of guessing.
Connects the incident to better observability and release readiness.
Explains why a scoped flag disable was safer than an automatic full rollback.
exampleStories.weakVersion: My release caused latency, so we rolled it back, watched the graphs recover, and added tests afterward.
followUpAngles: How did you know customers were affected?
What did you communicate before root cause was confirmed?
Why disable the flag instead of full rollback?
Which detection gap changed afterward?

exampleStories.title: Cache Stampede Fix-Forward
exampleStories.promptVariant: Describe a time when the first mitigation fixed one symptom but left another risk.
exampleStories.situation: A senior engineer introduced a cache-key change that looked safe in canary because the canary did not include tenant-scale imports. When a large tenant's nightly import started, API latency spiked, background jobs fell behind, and the first fix-forward attempt reduced latency but created duplicate notification jobs for about 1,800 users.
strongAnswerSketch: Declare the incident with the deploy and tenant-import timeline, then state clearly that their cache change was the likely trigger while keeping the discussion focused on impact.

Compare full rollback, rate-limiting the tenant import, and targeted cache prewarm plus worker throttling; choose throttling first because rollback would amplify job retries and duplicate notifications.

Notice the first mitigation's duplicate-job side effect from queue metrics and support examples, pause noncritical notifications, and publish the residual customer impact instead of declaring victory when latency recovered.
Coordinate with product and support on customer messaging for delayed and duplicate notifications, then reconcile queued jobs with an idempotency check.
Afterward, add a load test with tenant-scale imports, queue-depth and duplicate-job alerts, an idempotency requirement for notification workers, and a release note rule for cache-key changes.
whyItWorks: Makes the candidate's own triggering change explicit without collapsing into self-blame.
Shows that recovery was partial and that the candidate caught a second-order effect.
Compares mitigation alternatives under real operational trade-offs.
Treats customer communication, queue reconciliation, and idempotency as part of production ownership.
exampleStories.weakVersion: I found that my cache change caused a spike, pushed a quick fix, saw latency recover, and then added a load test so the same cache issue would not happen again.
followUpAngles: What made the canary miss this tenant-scale behavior?
Why not roll back immediately?
How did you detect that the first mitigation caused duplicate jobs?
What customer impact remained after API latency recovered?
What idempotency or rollout rule changed afterward?

exampleStories.title: Silent Data Drop
exampleStories.promptVariant: Describe a time something failed after release and the impact was not obvious at first.
exampleStories.situation: A new event-processing path dropped about 2 percent of analytics events when payloads contained a rare enum value. No alert fired because overall volume stayed within normal range, but a product experiment depended on the missing events.
strongAnswerSketch: Use replayable logs to estimate affected event types, time window, and dashboards that were misleading.
Coordinate with data and product to annotate affected metrics instead of silently backfilling and pretending nothing happened.
Build a safe replay for recoverable events and explicitly list events that could not be recovered.
Add dead-letter monitoring, schema-contract tests, and product-facing data freshness indicators.
whyItWorks: Treats data correctness as production impact.
Communicates business uncertainty instead of hiding it behind a technical fix.
Adds monitoring for silent failure, not only visible outage.
exampleStories.weakVersion: I fixed the enum handling bug, backfilled what I could, and told product the dashboards were accurate again.
followUpAngles: How did you estimate missing data?
Who needed to know the metrics were unreliable?
What could not be recovered?
What alert would catch this class of failure?

exampleStories.title: Runbook Gap During On-Call
exampleStories.promptVariant: Tell me about a time you improved observability, reliability, or performance.
exampleStories.situation: During an on-call week, a queue backlog caused delayed notifications. The immediate mitigation was known by one senior engineer, but the runbook was stale and the on-call engineer lost forty minutes finding the right lever.
strongAnswerSketch: Stabilize the backlog with the known-safe throttle, document the exact command used, and confirm customer impact stopped increasing.
Interview the on-call engineer while the details are fresh to understand which dashboard, alert, and runbook steps failed.
Update the runbook with decision thresholds, create a queue-age alert, and run a short game-day exercise.
Assign ownership for runbook review at each service's quarterly operational health check, including an expiry date for risky manual mitigations.
whyItWorks: Shows tech-lead scope: improving how others respond, not only fixing the current issue.
Uses the incident to expose knowledge concentration and stale documentation.
Creates a repeatable operational review habit.
Makes knowledge concentration and stale operational guidance visible as team-level risk.
exampleStories.weakVersion: I updated the runbook after the incident and reminded the team to keep documentation current so on-call would be faster next time.
followUpAngles: What did the runbook miss?
How did you validate the new steps?
What metric told you the backlog was customer-impacting?
How did ownership of runbooks change?

exampleStories.title: Risky Billing Status Data Repair
exampleStories.promptVariant: Describe a time when you pushed back on a risky production mitigation.
exampleStories.situation: A webhook retry bug left 614 renewal accounts with stale billing status. Support and revenue operations wanted an immediate SQL update from a spreadsheet because some customers could not renew, but the spreadsheet mixed tenant IDs, contract exceptions, and accounts already corrected by a retry.
strongAnswerSketch: State the customer and revenue impact, suspected webhook failure window, and why the proposed direct update could corrupt accounts that were already correct.
Refuse the one-off SQL path in the incident channel, but pair that refusal with a safer plan: dry-run diff, billing-owner review, backup table, sampled validation, and a reversible correction script.
Escalate to the incident lead and billing service owner for the approval decision instead of turning the disagreement into a private argument with support.
Use a temporary manual override for the highest-value blocked renewals while the correction script is reviewed, and publish the extra delay and residual risk clearly.
After recovery, add webhook idempotency coverage, stale-status alerting, and a production data-change checklist with approval thresholds and rollback notes.
whyItWorks: Rewards restraint without making the candidate passive or obstructionist.
Shows escalation with evidence, ownership, and a concrete safer path.
Makes the trade-off visible: a slower correction protected data integrity while temporary overrides reduced customer pain.
Converts a risky manual mitigation into a durable production-change mechanism.
exampleStories.weakVersion: Support wanted a data fix, so I asked my manager if it was safe, waited for approval, ran the update, and later added a test for the webhook bug.
followUpAngles: What exactly made the fast SQL update unsafe?
How did you avoid simply blocking support?
Who had authority to approve the correction?
What customer pain continued while you chose the safer path?
What production data-change rule changed afterward?

strongAnswerPattern.summary: A strong production story shows structured response, honest communication, accountable mitigation, and operational learning that changes future behavior.
moves: Starts with impact, severity, affected users, and current owner.
Uses observability and recent changes to narrow the problem systematically.
Communicates knowns, unknowns, next update time, and customer implications.
Makes mitigation trade-offs explicit instead of treating rollback or fix-forward as automatic.
Pushes back on unsafe fast fixes with evidence and a concrete alternative.
Owns the candidate's contribution without claiming credit for the whole incident response.
Names residual impact after the main symptom recovers, such as data cleanup, delayed work, or customer communication debt.
Improves detection, rollback, runbooks, tests, idempotency, or ownership afterward.

weakAnswerPattern.summary: A weak answer over-focuses on debugging heroics, quick rollback, or self-defense and misses customer impact, communication, residual risk, or prevention.
redFlags: The candidate cannot state customer impact or incident severity.
They describe a technical timeline but not their decisions or communication.
They blame the person who shipped the change or the team that owned the dependency.
They claim the fix solved everything but cannot name residual impact, detection, or prevention work.
They hide uncertainty from stakeholders until root cause is fully known.
They say the graph recovered but cannot explain residual data, queue, support, or customer cleanup.
They perform or approve risky production changes because the request is urgent without a dry run, owner, or rollback path.
They describe being blamed or being innocent more than the operational decisions they made.

followUps.question: How did you determine customer or business impact during the issue?

strong: We used checkout p95 latency by segment, support contacts, and order-completion rate; error rate alone was misleading because requests still succeeded slowly.
For the data issue, I estimated affected event types and time window from replayable logs, then marked downstream dashboards as unreliable.
For the cache incident, I separated API latency recovery from queued-job impact, duplicate notifications, and tenant-import delay.
weak: The graphs looked bad, so we knew it was important.

followUps.question: What mitigation alternatives did you consider?

strong: We compared full rollback, disabling the promotions flag, and throttling calls; disabling the flag removed the latency while preserving trace data and avoiding a wider rollback.
For the event issue, we paused the new path, replayed recoverable events, and clearly documented the unrecoverable slice instead of fabricating complete data.
For the cache issue, rollback looked clean but would have retried the tenant import and duplicated more jobs, so we throttled workers first and paused noncritical notifications.
weak: We rolled back because rollback is safest.
We fixed forward because we wanted to avoid more disruption.

followUps.question: When did you decide not to take the fastest-looking mitigation?

strong: Support wanted a direct SQL repair, but the source spreadsheet mixed corrected and uncorrected accounts, so I proposed a dry-run diff, billing-owner approval, backup table, and sampled validation instead.
We delayed the data repair by about forty minutes, but used temporary overrides for the highest-value blocked renewals so customer pain did not wait for a perfect process.
I escalated the decision to the incident lead and service owner with the blast radius, safer path, and residual customer impact rather than arguing privately or simply refusing.
weak: I did not feel comfortable making the production change, so I waited for a manager to decide.
We were under pressure, so we made the data update and planned to clean up anything wrong afterward.

followUps.question: What did you communicate while root cause was still uncertain?

strong: I posted the affected endpoint, latency symptom, suspected release window, what we had ruled out, and the next update time.
I told product the dashboard data for two reports was unreliable for the window and that we would annotate, estimate, and recover what we could.
I said my cache-key change was the likely trigger, API latency was recovering, and we were still validating queue delay and duplicate notifications before calling the incident resolved.
weak: I waited until we understood the root cause so we would not confuse people.
I kept people updated that we were investigating.

strong: Checkout now alerts on customer-visible latency, and promotion-heavy carts are part of performance testing before release.
The queue runbook now has thresholds, owner review dates, and a game-day check rather than just a generic restart step.
Cache-key changes now require tenant-scale load tests, notification idempotency checks, and rollback notes for queue side effects.
Production data repairs now require dry-run output, peer review, approval threshold, rollback or reconciliation notes, and a named customer-correction owner.
weak: The team agreed to be more careful before releases.

signals.name: Structured Response
signals.strong: Works from impact, evidence, ownership, rejected options, and mitigation trade-offs rather than panic or guesswork.
signals.weak: Narrates debugging activity without clear severity, decision-making, ownership, or alternatives considered.

signals.name: Communication Under Uncertainty
signals.strong: Communicates confirmed facts, uncertainty, next steps, customer implications, and residual impact clearly.
signals.weak: Waits for full certainty, gives vague updates, creates false confidence, or declares recovery before cleanup is understood.

signals.name: Boundary and Escalation Judgment
signals.strong: Pushes back on unsafe production actions with evidence, a decision owner, and a safer mitigation path.
signals.weak: Treats escalation as waiting for someone else, or accepts risky production changes because the request is urgent.

signals.name: Operational Learning
signals.strong: Improves detection, rollback, runbooks, tests, idempotency, or ownership in a verified way.
signals.weak: Ends at the fix or adds generic logging without tying it to the failure mode or verifying action-item closure.

rubric.expected: Contributes calmly to diagnosis or mitigation, communicates evidence, acknowledges their part when relevant, flags unsafe shortcuts, and owns a clear follow-up.
Frames impact, rejected options, residual customer cost, and trade-offs; coordinates across owners; safely handles data or rollback risk; and turns root cause into stronger operational safeguards.
Improves team response capability through runbooks, dashboards, game days, ownership, rollback and production-change decision rules, and incident-review discipline.

prompts.label: What failed, who was affected, and how did you know?
What role did you personally play in response or recovery?
How did you diagnose, mitigate, communicate, coordinate, and choose among imperfect options?
What customer impact stopped, what residual impact remained, and what outcome changed?
What did you learn about production ownership?
What detection, runbook, release, rollback, or reliability mechanism changed?

relatedScenarios: A release creates latency without increasing error rate.
A data pipeline silently drops a small percentage of events.
A stale runbook slows on-call recovery.
A feature flag, rollback, or throttle decision requires a trade-off during incident response.
A stakeholder asks for a direct production data edit before blast radius, approval, and rollback are clear.
A candidate-authored change causes an incident and the first mitigation leaves residual cleanup.
An incident appears recovered on service dashboards while queues, data, support tickets, or customer communication still need closure.
